label: remark: unknown mean
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark: unknown mean}
    Centering is for notational clarity. If $Y_i^{\rm raw}=\mu + \Lambda \eta_i + \epsilon_i$ with unknown $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^D$, we center by $\widehat\mu=\overline Y$. More generally, let $m_g=\mathbb{E}_g[\eta_i]$ and $V_g={\sf Cov}_g(\eta_i)$ be positive definite. The transformation
$$\eta_i^* = V_g^{-1/2}(\eta_i - m_g), \qquad \Lambda^*=\Lambda V_g^{1/2}, \qquad \mu^*=\mu + \Lambda m_g$$
leaves the distribution unchanged and gives $\mathbb{E}[\eta_i^*]=0$ and ${\sf Cov}(\eta_i^*)=I_d$. Thus these normalizations are without loss of generality. With $H=I_n - n^{-1}\mathbf 1_n\mathbf 1_n^\top$, the centered data satisfy
    $$HY^{\rm raw} = (HM) \Lambda^\top + HE.$$
    Sample centering removes only the intercept direction and replaces $\eta_i$ by $\eta_i-\overline\eta$, and $\epsilon_i$ by $\epsilon_i-\overline \epsilon$. Appendix \ref{app: sample centering} shows that the spectral-recovery and density-estimation rates in Sections \ref{subsec: spectral recovery}, \ref{subsec: latent density upper bound}, and \ref{subsec: obs density upper bound} are unchanged. We therefore use the centered formulation throughout.

title: Notation
body_md: For $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Vector and matrix norms are generally Euclidean and spectral, respectively, with $\|\cdot\|_F$ denoting the Frobenius norm; $s_k(A)$ is the $k$th largest singular value of $A$. The orthogonal group is $\mathcal{O}(d)$. We write $a_{n,D}\lesssim b_{n,D}$ when $a_{n,D}\leq Cb_{n,D}$ for a constant independent of $n,D$ but possibly depending on fixed model-class constants and $d$, and write $a_{n,D}\asymp b_{n,D}$ when both inequalities hold. Lastly, $a_{n,D}\ll b_{n,D}$ or $a_{n,D}=o(b_{n,D})$ denotes $a_{n,D}/b_{n,D}\to 0$.

body_md:
\label{remark: uniform upper bound}
    Let the class of all parameters satisfying the stated assumptions be denoted as $\Theta_*=\{\theta=(g,\Lambda, \Sigma): \theta \text{ satisfies}$ $\text{Assumptions } \ref{assume: loadings}- \ref{assume: smoothness of g_0}\}$. Then, the results in Theorems \ref{thm: spectral recovery} and \ref{thm: new kde} can be stated uniformly over $\Theta_*$, with constants depending only on $d,\beta, L$, the fixed constants in the factor-model assumptions, and the kernel norms. In particular, for the latent density estimation results, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every $\theta\in\Theta_*$, there is a measurable rotation $R_\theta\in\mathcal{O}(d)$ and an event $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}(\theta)$ satisfying $\inf_{\theta\in \Theta_*} \mathbb{P}_\theta \{\mathcal{E}_{n,D}(\theta)\}\geq 1-C/n$, for which, for any deterministic bandwidth $h>0$, we have
    $$\mathbb{E}_\theta [\|\widehat g_h - g^{R_\theta}\|_{L^2}^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}(\theta)] \leq C\mathcal{R}_{n,D}(h),$$
    where $\mathcal{R}_{n,D}(h)$ is given in Equation \eqref{eq: kde upper bound full}. Consequently, this implies the uniform bound $\sup_{\theta\in \Theta_*} \mathbb{E}_\theta d_{\mathcal{O}}^2(\widehat g, g) \leq C \mathcal{R}_{n,D}(h)$. To see this uniformity, note that although the event $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$ itself depends on $\theta$, its probability guarantee is uniform as all the concentration events in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery} depend only on the constants in the assumptions and $d$, which are fixed. For the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: new kde}, all constants depend on the relevant concentration events, whose probabilities are controlled uniformly via the assumptions on the parameters, the kernel norms, and $\|g\|_{L^2}^2$, which is bounded by Parseval's inequality $\|g\|_{L^2}^2\lesssim \int |\varphi_g(t)|^2 dt \leq L^2$ by Assumption \ref{assume: smoothness of g_0}. Therefore, we shall henceforth write $\mathcal{R}_{\rm FADE}(n,D)$ to denote the uniform bound $\sup_{\theta\in \Theta_*} \mathbb{E}_\theta [d_{\mathcal{O}}^2(\widehat{g}_{h^*}, g)]\lesssim \mathcal{R}_{\rm FADE}(n,D)$, where $h^*$ is the optimized bandwidth discussed in the next section and $\widehat{g}_h$ is the FADE density estimator constructed from $n$ observations $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Part A: } (Control for $\Lambda$ part) From the proof (step 5) of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i), we have 
    $$\|\hat{\Lambda} - \Lambda_0 R\|_F \leq A_1 + A_2 + B_1 + B_2,$$
    see Equations \eqref{eq: point estimate Lambda decompose}, \eqref{eq: point estimate Lambda decompose A} and \eqref{eq: point estimate Lambda decompose B}. We bound the four terms separately.

    For $A_1$, exactly as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i), 
    $$A_1 \lesssim \sqrt{D}(1/n + 1/D) \text{ on } \mathcal{E}_{n,D} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbb{E}_0[A_1^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}] \lesssim D(1/n+1/D)^2.$$

    For $A_2$, following the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i), we get
    $$A_2 \leq \|\Lambda_0\|_F \left\|\frac{\bar{D}_0}{\sqrt{n}} - I_d\right\| \lesssim \sqrt{D} \left\|\frac{\bar{D}_0}{\sqrt{n}} - I_d\right\|.$$
    Since the rows of $M_0$ are iid sub-Gaussian, centered with covariance $I_d$, and $d$ is fixed, the usual sample covariance moment bound gives
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\|(1/n)M_0^\top M_0 - I_d\|^2 \lesssim 1/n \Longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_0[A_2^2] \lesssim D  \frac1n.$$
    Since $\mathbb{P}_0(\mathcal{E}_{n,D})\geq 1 - c/n$, 
    $$\mathbb{E}_0[A_2^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}] \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}_0[A_2^2]}{\mathbb{P}_0(\mathcal{E}_{n,D})}\lesssim \frac{D}{n}.$$
    Thus,
    $$\mathbb{E}_0[(A_1+A_2)^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}] \lesssim D\left(\frac1D + \frac1n\right)^2 + \frac{D}{n} \lesssim \frac{D}{n} + \frac1D.$$

    Now, for $B_1$, we had
    $$B_1 \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \|E_0^\top U_0\|_F$$
    since $\|U_0^\top U\|\leq 1$. Conditional on $M_0$, $U_0^\top \epsilon^{(j)}\sim N_d(0, \sigma_{0j}^2 I_d)$ and hence $\mathbb{E}_0[\|U_0^\top \epsilon^{(j)}\|^2 \mid M_0] = d\sigma_{0j}^2$. Since the true noise variances are uniformly bounded, $\mathbb{E}\|E_0^\top U_0\|_F^2 = \sum_{j=1}^D \mathbb{E}\|U_0^\top \epsilon^{(j)}\|^2 \lesssim D$. This gives
    $$\mathbb{E}_0[B_1^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}] \lesssim \frac{D}{n}.$$

    For $B_2$, we already had the pointwise bound $B_2\lesssim \sqrt{D}(1/n+1/D)$ on $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$ and hence 
    $$\mathbb{E}_0[B_2^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}] \lesssim D\left(\frac1n + \frac1D\right)^2 \lesssim \frac{D}{n^2} + \frac1D.$$

    Combining all the parts and applying Jensen's inequality, we have
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\|\hat{\Lambda} - \Lambda_0 R\|_F\mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right] \lesssim \sqrt{\frac{D}{n}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}.$$

    \medskip\noindent
    \textbf{Part B: } (Control for $\Sigma$ part) As in Step 3(b) in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i), we have
    $$|\widehat{\sigma}_j^2 - \sigma_{0j}^2| \leq Q_j + |T_{j,1}| + |T_{j,2}| + |T_{j,3}|, \quad Q_j = \left|\frac1n \epsilon^{(j)\top} P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)} - \sigma_{0j}^2 \right|,$$
    see Equations \eqref{eq: sigma error} and \eqref{eq: T decomposition}. 

    For $Q_j$, note that conditional on $M_0$, $P_0^\perp$ is fixed with rank $n-d$ and independent of $\epsilon^{(j)}$. Therefore, $\epsilon^{(j)\top}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)} / \sigma_{0j}^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-d}$. Consequently,
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\frac1n \epsilon^{(j)\top}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)} - \sigma_{0j}^2 \mid M_0\right]=-\frac{d\sigma_{0j}^2}{n}, \; {\sf Var}_0\left(\frac1n \epsilon^{(j)\top}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)} - \sigma_{0j}^2 \mid M_0\right)=\frac{2(n-d)\sigma_{0j}^4}{n^2}.$$

    Since $d$ is fixed and the noise variances are uniformly bounded, $\mathbb{E}_0[Q_j^2] \lesssim 1/n$, and hence, $\mathbb{E}_0[\sum_j Q_j^2]\lesssim D/n$. Since $\mathbb{P}_0(\mathcal{E}_{n,D})\geq 1-c/n$, we have 
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\sum_{j=1}^D Q_j^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right] \lesssim \frac{D}{n}.$$


    
    For $T_{j,1}$, the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i) shows $|T_{j,1}|\lesssim (1/n+1/D)\|\lambda_{0j}\|^2$ uniformly over $j$ on $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$. Thus,
    $$\sum_j T_{j,1}^2 \lesssim \left(\frac1n + \frac1D\right)^2 \sum_{j=1}^D \|\lambda_{0j}\|^4.$$
    Under the loading assumptions, $\max_j \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2 \lesssim \ell_D$ and $\sum_j \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2 = \|\Lambda_0\|_F^2 \lesssim D$. Hence, $\sum_j \|\lambda_{0j}\|^4 \lesssim D\ell_D$. This gives
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[ \sum_{j=1}^D T_{j,1}^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right] \lesssim D \ell_D\left(\frac{1}{n^2} + \frac{1}{D^2}\right).$$

    For $T_{j,3}$, by \eqref{eq: sigma T_j3 decompose}, we have
    $$|T_{j,3}| \leq \frac2n \|U_0^\top \epsilon^{(j)}\| \|E_U\| \|\epsilon^{(j)}\| + \frac1n \|E_U\|^2 \|\epsilon^{(j)}\|^2.$$
    On $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$, $\|E_U\|\lesssim 1/\sqrt{n} + 1/\sqrt{D}$. Hence
    $$T_{j,3}^2 \lesssim \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\frac1n + \frac1D\right) \|U_0^\top \epsilon^{(j)}\|^2 \|\epsilon^{(j)}\|^2 + \frac{1}{n^2} \left(\frac1n + \frac1D\right)^2 \|\epsilon^{(j)}\|^4, \quad \text{on } \mathcal{E}_{n,D}.$$
    Since $U_0$ is independent of $E_0$, $d$ is fixed, and the noise variances are uniformly bounded,
    $$\mathbb{E}_0[\|U_0^\top \epsilon^{(j)}\|^2 \|\epsilon^{(j)}\|^2\mid M_0] \lesssim n, \quad \mathbb{E}_0\|\epsilon^{(j)}\|^4 \lesssim n^2.$$
    Using this in the last display, and summing over $j$,
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\sum_{j=1}^D T_{j,3}^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right] \lesssim \frac{D}{n}(1/n+1/D) + D(1/n + 1/D)^2 \lesssim \frac{D}{n} + \frac1D.$$
    

    Finally, for $T_{j,2}$ use the decomposition $T_{j,2}=T_{j,2}^{\rm linear} + T_{j,2}^{\rm rem}$ from \eqref{eq: sigma T_j2 decompose}. For the remainder, Equation \eqref{eq: bound remainder P-P0 decomposition} gives $\|\mathcal{R}(E_0)\|\lesssim 1/n + 1/D$ on $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$. Using $\|M_0\lambda_{0j}\|\lesssim \sqrt{n} \|\lambda_{0j}\|$ on $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$, we have $|T_{j,2}^{\rm rem}|\lesssim (1/n+1/D) \|\lambda_{0j}\| \|\epsilon^{(j)}\|/\sqrt{n}$. Thus, $\mathbb{E}_0[(T_{j,2}^{\rm rem})^2 \mathbbm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{n,D})] \lesssim (1/n+1/D)^2 \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2$. Summing over $j$, we get
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\sum_{j=1}^D (T_{j,2}^{\rm rem})^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right] \lesssim D\left(\frac{1}{n^2} + \frac{1}{D^2}\right).$$
    

    For the linear part, the argument in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i) gives
    $$T_{j,2}^{\rm linear} = -\frac2n \sum_{k=1}^D w_{jk} \epsilon^{(k)\top} P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)}, \quad \|w_j\|^2\lesssim \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2/D, \;|w_{jj}| \lesssim \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2/D.$$

    For the diagonal part, $L_{j,\rm diag} = -(2/n)w_{jj}\epsilon^{(j)\top}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)}.$
    Since $\mathbb{E}_0[((1/n)\epsilon^{(j)}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)})^2]\lesssim 1$, we obtain $\mathbf{E}_0 L_{j,\rm diag}^2 \lesssim \|\lambda_{0j}\|^4/D^2$. Therefore,
    $$\sum_{j=1}^D \mathbb{E}_0[L_{j,\rm diag}^2] \lesssim \frac{1}{D^2} \sum_{j=1}^D \|\lambda_{0j}\|^4 \lesssim \frac{\ell_D}{D}.$$

    For the off-diagonal part, $L_{j, \rm off} = -(2/n) \sum_{k\neq j} w_{jk} \epsilon^{(k)\top}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)}.$ Conditional on $M_0$ and $\epsilon^{(j)}$, the variables $\epsilon^{(k)\top}P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)}$ ($k\neq j$) are independent centered Gaussian variables. Hence
    $$\mathbb{E}_0[L_{j,\rm off}^2 \mid M_0, \epsilon^{(j)}] \lesssim \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{k\neq j} w_{jk}^2 \|P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)}\|^2 \lesssim \frac{\|w_j\|^2}{n^2} \|P_0^\perp \epsilon^{(j)}\|^2.$$
    Taking expectation over $\epsilon^{(j)}$, $\mathbb{E}_0[L_{j,\rm off}^2] \lesssim \|w_j\|^2/n \lesssim \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2 / (nD)$. Summing over $j$,
    $$\sum_{j=1}^D \mathbb{E}_0[L_{j,\rm off}^2] \lesssim \frac{1}{nD} \sum_{j=1}^D \|\lambda_{0j}\|^2 \lesssim \frac1n.$$

    Combining all the bounds from the different parts, simplifying and using $\ell_D \lesssim n$ (since $\ell_D\lesssim \sqrt{n \log(nD)}$ and $\log(nD)\lesssim n$), we have
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\|\hat{\Sigma} - \Sigma_0\|_F^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D} \right] \lesssim \frac{D}{n} + \frac{\ell_D}{D}.$$
    Application of Jensen's inequality gives the result we set to prove.

body_md:
\label{thm: weak kde g0}
    Suppose we construct estimator $\hat{g}_h$ using a kernel $K$ with bandwidth $h$ from the pre-estimated factors in $\widehat{M}$. Assuming \eqref{assume: dimensions}--\eqref{assume: latent tail}, with $g_0$ of smoothness $\beta$, and normalized, integrable, spherically symmetric $K\in C^1\cap L^2$ of order $\beta$ with $\nabla K\in L^2$, then
        $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\|\hat{g}_h - g_0^R\|_{L^2}^2\mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right] \lesssim h^{2\beta} + \frac{1}{nh^d} + \frac{1}{Dh^{d+2}} + \frac{\log n}{nh^{d+2}}.$$
    Here, $\mathcal{E}_{n,D}$ is the event in Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery}(i). The constants appearing in $\lesssim$ are based on constants depending on $g_0$ and $K$, and thus free of $n$ or $D$. Using this upper bound, taking $h^*\asymp (\frac1D+\frac{\log n}{n})^{1/(2\beta+d+2)}$ yields the following rate:
    $$\mathbb{E}_0\left[\|\hat{g}_{h^*} - g_0^R\|_{L^2}^2 \mid \mathcal{E}_{n,D}\right]\lesssim  \left(\frac1D + \frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+d+2}}.$$

name: Concentration of $\xi_i$

title: Proof
body_md:
Finally, recall $\xi_i = \sqrt{n}S_0^{-1}V_0^\top E_0^\top P_0^\perp e_i$. Note that $\mathbb{E}_0[\xi_i]=\mathbb{E}_0[\xi_i\mid\mathbf{M}_0]=0$. Further, ${\sf Cov}(\xi_i\mid\mathbf{M}_0)=\mathbb{E}_0[\xi_i\xi_i^\top\mid\mathbf{M}_0]=(P_0^\perp)_{ii}\Sigma_\xi$, where $\Sigma_\xi = nS_0^{-1}V_0^\top\Sigma_0V_0S_0^{-1}$. The $\xi_i'$s are not conditionally independent, but on $\mathcal{E}_{\eta}$ (see Step 1(a) in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: new kde}), we have $\|{\sf Cov}(\xi_i\mid \mathbf{M}_0)\|\lesssim 1/D$. Hence, $\mathbb{E}_0[\|\xi_i\|^2\mid \mathbf{M}_0]\leq \text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi)\lesssim 1/D$ on $\mathcal{E}_\eta$. Thus, 
    $$\xi_i\mid \mathbf{M}_0 \sim N_d(0, (P_0^\perp)_{ii}\Sigma_\xi).$$
    Applying Hanson-Wright inequality for Gaussian vectors, we have
    $$\mathbb{P}_0\left(\|\xi_i\|^2 - \mathbb{E}_0[\|\xi_i\|^2\mid \mathbf{M}_0] \geq 2\sqrt{\text{tr}\left(((P_0^\perp)_{ii}\Sigma_\xi)^2\right)t} + 2\|(P_0^\perp)_{ii}\Sigma_\xi\|t \mid \mathbf{M}_0\right)\leq e^{-t}.$$
    Using $(P_0^\perp)_{ii}\leq 1$ and the $\mathbb{E}_0[\|\xi_i\|^2\mid \mathbf{M}_0]\leq \text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi)$, we get
    $$\mathbb{P}_0\left(\|\xi_i\|^2 - \text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi) \geq 2\sqrt{\text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi^2)t} + 2\|\Sigma_\xi\|t\mid \mathbf{M}_0\right) \leq e^{-t}.$$

    Since the event $\mathcal{E}_\eta$ depends solely on $\mathbf{M}_0$, its indicator $\mathbbm{1}(\mathcal{E}_\eta)$ is $\mathbf{M}_0-$measureable. Thus, application of union bound (and integrating out the randomness of $\mathbf{M}_0$) gives
    $$\mathbb{P}\left(\left\{\max_i \|\xi_i\|^2 \geq \text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi) + 2\sqrt{\text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi^2)t} + 2\|\Sigma_\xi\|t\right\} \cap \mathcal{E}_\eta\right) \leq \mathbb{E}_\eta\left[\sum_{i=1}^n e^{-t}\mathbbm{1}(\mathcal{E}_\eta)\right].$$
    Setting $t=\log(n/\varepsilon)$ fixes the total failure probability of the union bound to $\varepsilon$. Now, on $\mathcal{E}_{\eta}$, we can use $\|\Sigma_\xi\|\leq C_0/D$, hence $\text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi)\leq dC_0/D$ and $\text{tr}(\Sigma_\xi^2)\leq dC_0^2/D^2$. Plugging these back, we get that with probability 
    $$\mathbb{P}_0\left(\left\{\max_i \|\xi_i\|^2 \geq \frac{C_0}{D}[d + 2\sqrt{d\log(n/\varepsilon)} + 2\log(n/\varepsilon)] \right\} \cap \mathcal{E}_\eta\right) \leq \varepsilon.$$
    Hence, the result follows. 

    \textbf{Note:} Plugging in $\varepsilon=1/n$, we get that $\max_i\|\xi_i\| \lesssim \sqrt{\frac{\log n}{D}}$ holds with probability at least $1-c/n$ for some $c>0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Starting with the form of $\mathcal{R}_{n,D}(h)$ from Theorem \ref{thm: new kde}, use $(a+b)^k\lesssim a^k +b^k$ for $k=2,4,6$ on $\rho_{n,D}$. Write $a_{n,D}=\sqrt{\log(nD)}/D$ and $b_n=(\log n)/\sqrt{n}$, and $q=2\beta+d+6$.

        First, we argue that the terms carrying an additional factor $n^{-1}$ do not introduce new bandwidth scales. Because $h^* \geq h_{D,1}$, $h^* \geq D^{-1/(\beta+2)}\geq D^{-1/2}$ for $D$ sufficiently large. Hence
        $$\frac{1}{nD(h^*)^{d+2}}\leq \frac{1}{n(h^*)^d}, \quad \frac{1}{nD^2(h^*)^{d+4}} \leq \frac{1}{n(h^*)^d}.$$

        Likewise, since $h^*\geq a_{n,D}^{1/(\beta+1)}=h_{D,2}$ and $h^*\geq b_n^{1/(\beta+1)}=h_{n,1}$ and $a_{n,D}, b_n = o(1)$, we have $a_{n,D} \lesssim h^*$ and $b_n\lesssim h^*$. Consequently,
        $$\frac{\rho_{n,D}^2}{n(h^*)^{d+2}} \lesssim \frac{1}{n(h^*)^d}, \quad \frac{\rho_{n,D}^4}{n(h^*)^{d+4}} \lesssim \frac{1}{n(h^*)^d}.$$
        Moreover, $\rho_{n,D}^4/(h^*)^4 \lesssim \rho_{n,D}^2/(h^*)^2$ as $\rho_{n,D} \lesssim h^*$. Therefore, it is enough to control the terms
        $$h^{2\beta}, \; \frac{1}{nh^d}, \; \frac{1}{D^2h^4},\; \frac{a_{n,D}^2}{h^2}, \; \frac{b_n^2}{h^2}, \; \frac{\log^3 n}{D^3 h^{d+6}}, \; \frac{a_{n,D}^6}{h^{d+6}}, \; \frac{b_n^6}{h^{d+6}}.$$
        Balancing each decreasing term with $h^{2\beta}$ gives precisely the bandwidths in the corollary. Since $h^*$ is at least each of these balancing bandwidths, every term in the preceding display is bounded by a constant multiple of $(h^*)^{2\beta}$, which implies $R(h^*)\lesssim (h^*)^{2\beta}$.

label: lemma: moment correction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: moment correction}
    There exist bounded, smooth, even functions $b_0,\dots,b_d$ depending only on $d$, such that for every sufficiently large $T$, one can choose coefficients $c_k(T)=O((1+T^2)e^{-T^2/2})$ for which
    $$F_T(x):= \cos(Tx_1) - \sum_{k=0}^d c_k(T) b_k(x)$$
    satisfies
    $$\mathbb{E} [F_T(X)] = 0, \quad \mathbb{E} [X_j^2 F_T(X)] = 0, \quad j=1,\dots, d.$$
    The functions may be chosen even in every coordinate, so $\mathbb{E}_0[X_j F_T(X)] = 0$ and all off-diagonal second moments vanish as well. Note all expectations are under $X\sim N(0,I_d)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To see this, choose bounded even $b_0,\dots,b_d$ for which the $(d+1)\times (d+1)$ matrix
    $$\left(\mathbb{E}[b_k(X)], \mathbb{E}[X_1^2 b_k(X)],\dots, \mathbb{E}[X_d^2 b_k(X)]\right)_{k=0}^d$$
    is nonsingular (call this matrix $M$). Such functions can be obtained, for example, by choosing $d+1$ points $z_0,\dots,z_d$ such that the vectors $(1, z_{k1}^2,\dots,z_{kd}^2)$ are linearly independent, and choose sufficiently localized even $C^\infty$ bumps around their coordinatewise sign orbits. Solving the resulting fixed finite-dimensional linear system $M c(T) = r(T)$ gives the coefficients $c_k(T)$, where $$r(T)=(\mathbb{E}[\cos(TX_1)], \mathbb{E}[X_1^2 \cos(TX_1)],\dots, \mathbb{E}[X_d^2\cos(TX_1)]).$$ Note that $\mathbb{E}[X_j^2 \cos(TX_1)]$ is $(1-T^2)e^{-T^2/2}$ for $j=1$ and $e^{-T^2/2}$ for $j\neq 1$, while $\mathbb{E}[\cos(TX_1)]=e^{-T^2/2}$ (using the characteristic function of standard normal), which implies $r(T)=e^{-T^2/2}(1, 1-T^2,1,\dots,1)$ and consequently $\|r(T)\|\lesssim (1+T^2)e^{-T^2/2}$. Thus, $\|c(T)\|\leq \|M^{-1}\|\|r(T)\|\lesssim (1+T^2)e^{-T^2/2}$. Hence, for every $k$
    $$|c_k(T) |\lesssim (1+T^2) e^{-T^2/2}.$$

label: lemma: subgaussian concentration
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: subgaussian concentration}[Sub-Gaussian concentration]
    Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix  whose rows $A_i$ are independent zero-mean sub-Gaussian isotropic random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then for any $t\geq 0$, we have
    $$\sqrt{m} - CK^2(\sqrt{n}+t)\leq s_{\min}(A)\leq s_{\max}(A)\leq \sqrt{m} + CK^2 (\sqrt{n}+t)$$
    with probability at least $1-2\exp(-t^2)$, where $K=\max_i \|A_i\|_{\psi_2}$. In fact, with the same probability, the following holds
    $$\left\|\frac{1}{m}A^\top A - I_n\right\|\leq K^2 \max\{\delta,\delta^2\}, \quad \delta = C(\sqrt{n/m} + t/\sqrt{m}).$$

label: thm: wedin
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: wedin}
    Let $A$ and $\tilde{A}=A + E$ be two $n\times D$ matrices. Let $A=UDV^\top + U_\perp D_\perp V_\perp^\top$ and $\tilde{A}=\tilde{U}\tilde{D}\tilde{V}^\top + \tilde{U}_\perp \tilde{D}_\perp\tilde{V}_\perp^\top$ be their respective SVD, where the first parts correspond to the top $d$ singular values. Let $\Phi_1 = \Theta(U, \tilde{U})$ and $\Phi_2 = \Theta(V, \tilde{V})$ be the canonical angles between the subspaces (as diagonal matrices). Additionally, suppose 
    $$s_d(\tilde{A}) \geq \alpha + \delta, \quad s_{d+1}(A) \leq \alpha$$
    for some $\alpha,\delta>0$. Then
    $$\max \{\|\sin\Phi_1\|, \|\sin\Phi_2\|\} \leq \frac{\|E\|}{\delta}.$$

label: lemma: positive correction preserves L1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: positive correction preserves L1}
    Let $\widehat g$ be an integrable, possibly signed function satisfying $\int \widehat g = 1$, and define $\widetilde g =\widehat g^+ / \int \widehat g^+$. Then, for every probability density $g$, we have
    $$\|\widetilde g - g \|_{L^1} \leq 2\|\widehat g - g\|_{L^1}.$$
    
    Moreover, for $\widehat g_h$ as in \eqref{eq: fade latent kde} for an integrable kernel $K$ satisfying $\int \|u\| |K(u)|du <\infty$, then,
    $$\int \|z\| \tilde{g}(z) dz \leq \sqrt{d} \|K\|_{L^1} + h\int \|u\| |K(u)| du.$$
    In particular, this first moment is uniformly bounded for $h\lesssim 1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery} to $Y^c$ gives the stated bounds initially with $M_{0,c}$ in place of $M_0$. The discussing preceding the proposition verifies all singular-value, Gaussian concentration, projection, and leave-one-out ingredients required by that proof.

    For the global score bound, use $M_{0,c}=M_0 - \mathbf 1_n \overline \eta^\top$ to obtain
    $$\|\widehat M - M_0 R\|_F \leq \|\widehat M - M_{0,c}R\|_F + \|\mathbf 1_n \overline \eta^\top R\|_F = \|\widehat M - M_{0,c}R\|_F + \sqrt n \|\overline \eta\|.$$
    By \eqref{eq: centered score concentration}, the additional term is $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, and is therefore absorbed by the existing $n-$dependent part of the bound.

    The centered rowwise expansion from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: spectral recovery} first gives
    $$\widehat \eta_i - R^\top (\eta_i - \overline \eta) = \widehat R^\top \xi_{i,c} + \widetilde \Delta_{i,c}$$
    with $\max_i \|\widetilde\Delta_{i,c}\| \lesssim \sqrt{\log (nD)}/D + (\log n)/\sqrt n$. Therefore, 
    $$\widehat \eta_i - R^\top \eta_i = \widehat R^\top \xi_{i,c} + \underbrace{\widetilde \Delta_{i,c} - R^\top \overline \eta}_{\Delta_{i,c}}$$
    where $\|\overline \eta\|\lesssim \sqrt{(\log n)/n}$ ensures that $\Delta_{i,c}$ has the stated uniform bound. 

    The loading proof is unchanged because the centered population signal retains the loading matrix $\Lambda_0$. For the residual variance estimator, sample centering removes one additional degree of freedom. The corresponding deterministic bias is $O(1/n)$, which is absorbed by the existing bounds for the noise variance estimation.
